  "title": "FrontierLoop: Diagnostic-Guided Mode Scheduling Between Data Generation and RL for Mathematical Self-Improvement",
  "core_problem": "Self-improvement methods for mathematical reasoning — where the model generates its own synthetic training data and improves without an external teacher — make scheduling decisions at the WRONG LEVEL OF ABSTRACTION. Existing adaptive methods tune hyperparameters WITHIN a single training paradigm (B-STaR adjusts temperature and reward thresholds within SFT iterations, ICLR 2025; AdaSTaR adjusts data sampling priorities within STaR, NeurIPS 2025), but the higher-level question of WHICH training paradigm to use at any given moment remains unanswered.

This matters because self-improvement involves two fundamentally different computational activities with different properties:

(1) DATA GENERATION (Support Expansion): Creating new synthetic training data — reasoning traces for existing problems (STaR-style) or entirely new problems (MathSmith/Absolute Zero-style). This is inference-only compute, expands the model's behavioral support (Unified View, arXiv 2604.07941), and its value depends on whether the current data pool has been exhausted.

(2) RL TRAINING (Policy Reshaping): Consolidating latent capabilities into reliable pass@1 performance via GRPO. This is gradient compute, reshapes the policy within the currently reachable behavior space, and its value depends on whether there is still a gap between what the model CAN do (pass@k) and what it reliably DOES (pass@1).

The optimal balance between these modes changes as the model improves, but no existing method adapts this balance:

- FIXED-PARADIGM METHODS (STaR, ReST-EM, SePT): Generate data, train, repeat on a fixed schedule. SePT (arXiv 2510.18814) alternates generation and SFT in fixed 3-epoch cycles without diagnostic guidance. ReST-EM observes diminishing returns after 2-3 iterations without understanding whether to generate more data or switch to RL.

- WITHIN-PARADIGM ADAPTIVE METHODS (B-STaR, AdaSTaR): Adapt hyperparameters within STaR/SFT. B-STaR (ICLR 2025) monitors exploration/exploitation via a balance score and adjusts temperature (0.5-1.2) and reward threshold — powerful levers WITHIN the SFT paradigm. But B-STaR cannot switch to RL training when the Sampling Efficiency Gap indicates consolidation would be more productive, and cannot generate new problems when its fixed training set is exhausted. AdaSTaR (NeurIPS 2025) uses solve-rate signals for adaptive data sampling with 58.6% FLOPs reduction — but adjusts WHICH data to sample, not WHETHER to generate new data or train differently.

- WITHIN-RL ADAPTIVE METHODS (SwS, SEC, SIRI): Adapt within RL training. SwS (NeurIPS 2025, arXiv 2506.08989) identifies weaknesses during RL and synthesizes targeted problems — but performs synthesis continuously, not diagnostically triggered. SIRI cycles rollout length within RL. SEC uses MAB for category selection within RL.

- CONTINUOUS SYNTHESIS (SvS): Synthesizes new problems at every RLVR step regardless of need, wasting compute when the current data pool is sufficient.

The key insight is that RL and data generation have COMPLEMENTARY failure modes: RL saturates when pass@k plateaus (it cannot expand the frontier beyond the base model's latent capabilities, arXiv 2504.13837), while data generation is wasteful when the model hasn't consolidated its existing knowledge (large Sampling Efficiency Gap means RL can still improve pass@1 without new data). The DIAGNOSTIC TOOLS to detect these states already exist — pass@64 predicts RL outcomes (Quagmires: R²=0.87 on Llama3-8B, arXiv 2510.01624), entropy trajectory signals collapse (Entrocraft, arXiv 2604.26326), and the generation-verification gap determines self-improvement ceilings (Mind the Gap, ICLR 2025) — but they have never been used for MODE-LEVEL scheduling between fundamentally different training regimes.",
  "opportunity": "We propose FrontierLoop: the first framework that uses diagnostic signals for MODE-LEVEL scheduling — switching between fundamentally different training regimes (data generation vs. RL) — in mathematical self-improvement. This extends prior work on within-paradigm adaptation (B-STaR's parameter adjustment, AdaSTaR's data selection) to the higher-level orchestration decision that determines the training regime itself.

The hierarchy of adaptive self-improvement decisions clarifies FrontierLoop's contribution:

Level 1 — TOKEN/GROUP-LEVEL: Pass@k Training (arXiv 2508.10751) computes group-level advantages to balance exploration/exploitation within single RL steps.
Level 2 — DATA-LEVEL: AdaSTaR adjusts which training examples to sample within iterations; HS-STaR targets boundary-difficulty problems; SAI-DPO (ACL 2026 Findings, arXiv 2505.16176) recalibrates instance selection using pass-rate difficulty.
Level 3 — PARAMETER-LEVEL: B-STaR adjusts temperature and reward thresholds across STaR iterations.
Level 4 — WITHIN-MODE: SwS synthesizes targeted problems within RL; SEC selects problem categories within RL; SIRI varies rollout length within RL.
Level 5 — MODE-LEVEL (FrontierLoop): Switches between fundamentally different computational regimes — inference-only data generation vs. gradient-based RL training — with different compute profiles, optimization objectives, and data requirements.

Four specific gaps at Level 5 create FrontierLoop's opportunity:

(a) NO MODE SWITCHING: B-STaR (ICLR 2025) is the strongest existing diagnostic-adaptive method, but it operates entirely within online RFT (SFT). It adjusts sampling temperature and reward threshold to balance exploration/exploitation — powerful levers within SFT. But B-STaR cannot switch to RL training when the Sampling Efficiency Gap indicates consolidation would be more productive, and cannot generate new problems when its fixed training set is exhausted. FrontierLoop adds the mode-switching capability that B-STaR lacks.

(b) FIXED-SCHEDULE CYCLING: SePT (arXiv 2510.18814) demonstrates that alternating between self-generation and training improves reasoning (Pass@1: 22.7→39.5 on Qwen2.5-Math-7B), but uses fixed 3-epoch cycles without diagnostics. Generation phases may occur when RL could still consolidate existing knowledge; training phases may continue past saturation. FrontierLoop replaces SePT's fixed schedule with diagnostic-triggered transitions.

(c) NO CROSS-MODE DIAGNOSTICS: SwS (NeurIPS 2025) diagnoses weaknesses WITHIN RL to guide problem synthesis, and B-STaR diagnoses exploration/exploitation WITHIN SFT to adjust parameters. But no method uses diagnostics to decide WHICH mode is currently most productive. When B-STaR detects declining exploration, its only lever is temperature — it cannot decide that switching to RL would be more effective.

(d) NO GENERATION-VERIFICATION GAP STOPPING: SOAR (arXiv 2601.18778) uses bilevel meta-RL where a teacher copy generates problems based on measured student progress, but requires a separate teacher-student architecture. The solver-verifier gap theory (arXiv 2507.00075) models self-improvement as an exponential curve toward a computable limit, but no method uses this for principled stopping of the overall self-improvement loop.

FrontierLoop's value proposition is COMPUTE EFFICIENCY through mode-appropriate scheduling: generate data only when diagnostics indicate frontier exhaustion (saving 20-30% over SePT's fixed generation), target generation at specific difficulty bands where the model is stuck, and consolidate via RL only when the Sampling Efficiency Gap indicates room for pass@1 improvement.",
  "landscape": "FOUNDATIONAL SELF-IMPROVEMENT METHODS:

STaR (arXiv 2203.14465, NeurIPS 2022, Zelikman et al.) generates chain-of-thought rationales, filters for correctness, and fine-tunes iteratively. Includes 'rationalization' for failed problems. FrontierLoop extends STaR's generate→filter→train loop with diagnostic-guided mode scheduling and RL-based consolidation.

ReST-EM (Beyond Human Data, arXiv 2312.06585, Google DeepMind, 2023) formalizes self-training as Expectation-Maximization. Critical observation: diminishing returns after 2-3 iterations. FrontierLoop uses diagnostics to distinguish genuine saturation from suboptimal data targeting.

V-STaR (arXiv 2402.06457, 2024) trains a DPO-based verifier on both correct and incorrect STaR solutions. FrontierLoop could incorporate V-STaR's verifier for enhanced filtering during generation phases.

DIAGNOSTIC-ADAPTIVE SELF-IMPROVEMENT — CLOSEST PRIOR WORK:

B-STaR (arXiv 2412.17256, ICLR 2025, HKUST) is the most directly relevant prior work. B-STaR monitors exploration (Pass@K, Pass@K-S, distinct equations) and exploitation (Best-of-K accuracy, Reward@K-S) across STaR iterations, computing a balance score bs_i = min(n'_i/n*, 1)·(n'_i/n_i) to autonomously adjust sampling temperature (0.5-1.2) and reward threshold (-1.0 to 1.0). On Mistral-7B, achieves GSM8K 53.8 and MATH 27.8 over 9 iterations. CRITICAL DIFFERENTIATION: B-STaR adapts parameters WITHIN a single training paradigm (online RFT/SFT). It does not generate new problems, does not incorporate RL training, and cannot switch between training modes. Its adaptation is at Level 3 (parameter adjustment); FrontierLoop operates at Level 5 (mode switching). B-STaR's insights are complementary — FrontierLoop could use B-STaR-style parameter adaptation WITHIN each mode while adding higher-level mode scheduling.

AdaSTaR (arXiv 2505.16322, NeurIPS 2025, Koh et al.) addresses data imbalance in STaR through adaptive sampling: a hierarchical min-heap priority system orders observations by last-sampled iteration and win-rate, with a curriculum component using training accuracy α as strength proxy (quadratic f(α)=α² for automatic difficulty scheduling). Achieves best accuracy on 6/6 benchmarks with 58.6% average FLOPs reduction. DIFFERENTIATION: AdaSTaR adapts WHICH data to sample (Level 2), not WHETHER to generate new data or switch training paradigms (Level 5). FrontierLoop's difficulty-stratified generation targeting extends AdaSTaR's adaptive sampling from within-iteration data selection to cross-mode generation decisions.

SAI-DPO (arXiv 2505.16176, ACL 2026 Findings) uses pass-rate-derived difficulty metrics and knowledge semantic alignment for iterative DPO training recalibration, achieving ~6 point improvements on AIME24. Operates within DPO training; FrontierLoop extends pass-rate-based adaptation to mode-level scheduling.

GENERATION↔TRAINING CYCLING METHODS:

SePT (arXiv 2510.18814, 'A Model Can Help Itself,' 2025) is the key ablation baseline. SePT alternates between self-generation (low-temperature sampling) and SFT training in FIXED 3-epoch cycles with online data refresh — each new batch from the most recently updated model. Temperature annealed 0.6→1.0. On Qwen2.5-Math-7B: Pass@1/8/32 of 39.5/57.7/67.9 (from 22.7/47.3/61.0 baseline). CRITICAL: SePT proves generation↔training cycling works but uses NO diagnostic guidance. It is the direct 'non-adaptive' version of FrontierLoop — showing FrontierLoop outperforms SePT demonstrates the value of diagnostic-guided mode scheduling.

SIRI (arXiv 2509.25176, 2025) performs 3 iterations of compression↔expansion cycling WITHIN RL, oscillating rollout length 8,192↔16,384 tokens via cosine scheduler. AIME24: 40.4% (vs. 28.2%) with 46.9% token reduction. SIRI cycles WITHIN RL (varying rollout length); FrontierLoop cycles BETWEEN modes (generation vs. RL).

ReMiT (arXiv 2602.03075, Feb 2026) performs iterative mid-training↔RL cycling across two cycles, validating that iterative cycling compounds.

WITHIN-RL PROBLEM SYNTHESIS:

SwS (arXiv 2506.08989, NeurIPS 2025) identifies questions the model consistently fails during RL, extracts core concepts, and synthesizes targeted problems. 10.0% avg improvement on 7B, 7.7% on 32B across 8 benchmarks. DIFFERENTIATION: SwS synthesizes WITHIN RL based on binary failure detection; FrontierLoop uses diagnostics for mode-level decisions (WHEN to synthesize at all) using multiple signals (pass@k spectrum, difficulty stratification, entropy).

Beyond Pass@1 / SvS (arXiv 2508.14029, 2025) synthesizes variational problems during RLVR, +18.3%/+22.8% pass@32 on AIME24/25. Continuous synthesis at every step; FrontierLoop's diagnostic-gated generation saves compute when current data is sufficient.

SOAR (arXiv 2601.18778, Meta FAIR/MIT/NYU, Jan 2026) uses bilevel meta-RL: a teacher COPY generates problems for a student copy, rewarded by measured student progress on hard problems (0/128 success rate). DIFFERENTIATION: SOAR requires separate teacher-student architecture; FrontierLoop uses a single model with diagnostic signals, lower compute overhead.

SELF-PLAY AND ZERO-DATA METHODS:

Absolute Zero (arXiv 2505.03335, 2025) achieves SOTA with zero external data via self-play. R-Zero (arXiv 2508.05004, 2025) uses Challenger-Solver co-evolution. R-Diverse (arXiv 2602.13103, Feb 2026) addresses 'Diversity Illusion.' FrontierLoop is generation-mechanism agnostic — self-play, sampling, or synthesis — with diagnostics determining which is productive.

DIAGNOSTIC TOOLS AND SIGNALS:

Quagmires (arXiv 2510.01624, NeurIPS 2025 MATH-AI Workshop) trained hundreds of models up to 12B: pass@64 predicts RL outcomes with R²=0.87, generalization loss achieves R²=0.88, combined predictor R²=0.94 (all on Llama3-8B-Instruct). Used as STATIC pre-RL predictor; FrontierLoop extends to DYNAMIC mode scheduling.

Pass@k Training (arXiv 2508.10751, ByteDance/RUC) uses pass@k as a GROUP-LEVEL reward signal: groups k responses, assigns positive reward if at least one correct, distributes group advantage to all k responses. 17.9% vs. 12.9% Pass@1 on Enigmata (Qwen2.5-7B). Validates pass@k as active signal at group-level granularity; FrontierLoop uses pass@k at phase-level diagnostic granularity for mode switching.

Entrocraft (arXiv 2604.26326, 2026) achieves ~17% improvement in pass@32 via entropy-guided rejection sampling. EntroPIC (arXiv 2511.15248, 2025) uses PID control for entropy stabilization. Both validate entropy trajectory as training stability diagnostic.

Cover@tau (arXiv 2510.08325, 2025) measures reasoning reliability beyond pass@k.

SELF-IMPROVEMENT THEORY:

Mind the Gap (arXiv 2412.02674, ICLR 2025) formalizes self-improvement through the generation-verification gap, scaling monotonically with pre-training compute. Provides FrontierLoop's stopping criterion.

Solver-Verifier Gap Theory (arXiv 2507.00075, 2025) models self-improvement as exponential curve toward computable limit. Key: external data can be introduced at any stage — supporting FrontierLoop's flexible scheduling.

'Can Large Reasoning Models Self-Train?' (arXiv 2505.21444) shows self-training improves then collapses via reward hacking. FrontierLoop's collapse detection addresses this.

Does RL Really Incentivize Reasoning Beyond the Base Model? (arXiv 2504.13837, NeurIPS 2025 Best Paper Runner-Up) shows RLVR improves pass@1 but does NOT expand pass@k frontier — FrontierLoop's central motivation for diagnostic-triggered generation.

DIFFICULTY-AWARE METHODS:

DART-Math (arXiv 2407.13690, NeurIPS 2024) identifies easy-query bias. HS-STaR (arXiv 2505.19866, EMNLP 2025) targets boundary problems. SEC (arXiv 2505.14970, 2025) uses MAB for curriculum within RL. MathSmith (arXiv 2508.05592, 2025) optimizes problem generation via RL. HSIR (arXiv 2605.24998, May 2026) improves within-iteration efficiency. All composable with FrontierLoop.

THEORETICAL FOUNDATIONS:

'Large Language Model Post-Training: A Unified View' (arXiv 2604.07941, Apr 2026) identifies support expansion, policy reshaping, behavioral consolidation. FrontierLoop's Generation=support expansion, RL=policy reshaping. 'Progress depends on coordinated systems design' motivates diagnostic-guided mode orchestration.

'Post-Training is About States, Not Tokens' (arXiv 2605.22731, May 2026) argues state distribution differentiates post-training methods. Supports FrontierLoop's mode scheduling across different state distributions.

RL on Incorrect Synthetic Data (arXiv 2406.14532, NeurIPS 2024) shows 8× efficiency on incorrect traces. Motivates using both correct and incorrect self-generated data in RL mode.",

  "approach": "We propose FrontierLoop, the first framework using diagnostic signals for MODE-LEVEL scheduling — switching between fundamentally different training regimes (data generation vs. RL) — in mathematical self-improvement. Unlike prior within-paradigm adaptation (B-STaR adjusts parameters within SFT; AdaSTaR adjusts data sampling within STaR; SwS synthesizes problems within RL), FrontierLoop makes the higher-level decision of WHICH training regime is most productive at any given moment.

FrontierLoop operates in the PURE SELF-IMPROVEMENT REGIME: no external teacher — the student generates its own synthetic data with only a mathematical answer verifier (standard for RLVR).

ARCHITECTURAL OVERVIEW: FrontierLoop alternates between two modes with qualitatively different compute profiles, governed by a diagnostic module:

MODE 1 — GENERATION (Frontier Expansion / Support Expansion): Generate new synthetic training data targeted at the model's current capability frontier. Three mechanisms, selectable by the scheduler: (a) SOLUTION SAMPLING: for problems at frontier difficulty, generate K solutions, filter for correctness (STaR-style); (b) VARIATIONAL PROBLEM SYNTHESIS: from correct solutions, synthesize structurally diverse problem variants (SvS-inspired); (c) WEAKNESS-TARGETED GENERATION: identify difficulty bands where pass@k stalls, generate new problems in those bands (extending SwS's within-RL weakness diagnosis to mode-level triggering). Within this mode, B-STaR-style temperature adaptation and AdaSTaR-style priority sampling can be applied — FrontierLoop's mode scheduling is orthogonal to and composable with within-mode adaptation.

MODE 2 — RL TRAINING (Consolidation / Policy Reshaping): GRPO-based RLVR on the accumulated data pool. Entropy management via Entrocraft-style annealing to prevent collapse. Both correct and incorrect traces used (RL on incorrect data is 8× more efficient, arXiv 2406.14532). Within this mode, SwS-style weakness detection and SEC-style category selection can operate — again orthogonal to mode scheduling.

DIAGNOSTIC MODULE: Evaluated on a compact held-out validation set (200 problems stratified by difficulty) every 100 training steps:

(1) SAMPLING EFFICIENCY GAP (SEG) = pass@k − pass@1 (k=32): When SEG is large, the model has latent capability that RL can consolidate → stay in RL. When SEG is small AND pass@k is low, the frontier is exhausted → switch to GENERATION. Building on Quagmires' validation (pass@64 predicts RL outcomes, R²=0.87 on Llama3-8B; combined predictor R²=0.94) and Pass@k Training's validation of pass@k as active group-level signal.

(2) DIFFICULTY-STRATIFIED FRONTIER SCORE (DSFS): Group validation problems into difficulty bands. Compute pass@32 per band. Identify bands where pass@32 stalls → target generation at those bands. Extends HS-STaR's boundary concept and AdaSTaR's solve-rate curriculum from within-iteration to cross-mode targeting.

(3) ENTROPY TRAJECTORY: Policy entropy during RL, compared against expected annealing schedule. Entropy below threshold signals collapse → trigger generation with elevated temperature (1.2-1.5) for diversity injection. Validated by Entrocraft and EntroPIC.

(4) SELF-CONSISTENCY DIVERGENCE (SCD): Gap between self-consistency accuracy (majority vote) and verified accuracy. Self-consistency rising while true accuracy plateaus → reward hacking (per arXiv 2505.21444). Trigger: pause RL, evaluate, reduce learning rate.

ADAPTIVE SCHEDULER — MODE SWITCHING LOGIC (z-score-normalized thresholds):
- IF SEG small (z < −1) AND pass@k stagnant (growth < ε per 500 steps) → Switch to GENERATION (frontier exhausted)
- IF SEG large (z > 0) AND entropy healthy → Stay in / switch to RL (consolidate)
- IF entropy below 0.8× scheduled value → DIVERSITY INJECTION: generation with elevated temperature
- IF SCD exceeds threshold → EMERGENCY PAUSE: checkpoint, evaluate, reduce learning rate
- IF pass@32 stagnant across ALL bands for 3 consecutive evaluations → STOP (generation-verification gap exhausted per Mind the Gap)

KEY DESIGN PRINCIPLE — COMPOSABILITY: FrontierLoop operates at Level 5 (mode scheduling) and is explicitly composable with methods at other levels. Within Generation Mode: AdaSTaR-style priority sampling (Level 2), B-STaR-style temperature adaptation (Level 3). Within RL Mode: SwS-style weakness detection (Level 4), SEC-style category selection (Level 4), Pass@k Training-style group rewards (Level 1). Each level addresses a different optimization granularity.

EXPERIMENTAL PLAN:

STAGE 0 — DIAGNOSTIC SIGNAL VALIDATION (1.5 weeks): Run a standard 3-iteration STaR loop on Qwen3-8B, logging all four diagnostic signals at every checkpoint. Analyze which signal best correlates with subsequent learning gain, signal-to-noise ratio, and lead time for stagnation/collapse detection.

STAGE 0.5 — CYCLING VALIDATION GATE (1.5 weeks): Single-cycle test: (i) RL until diagnostic indicates frontier exhaustion → plateau pass@32 = P1; (ii) Difficulty-targeted generation → create frontier data; (iii) Second RL phase → pass@32 = P2. GO/NO-GO: If P2 > P1 + 1pp on MATH-500, cycling validated → proceed. If not → PIVOT to single-iteration diagnostic-guided self-improvement (still novel at mode-scheduling level).

STAGE 1 — FULL EXPERIMENTS (4-5 weeks): FrontierLoop for up to 5 adaptive cycles, scheduler determines each phase's duration and total cycle count.

CORE BASELINES (7): (1) STaR with fixed 3 iterations; (2) ReST-EM with fixed 2 iterations; (3) Pure RLVR (GRPO, no generation); (4) Absolute Zero self-play; (5) SePT fixed-schedule generation↔SFT cycling (KEY BASELINE — non-adaptive FrontierLoop); (6) SvS continuous problem synthesis during RLVR; (7) B-STaR-style adaptive STaR (adaptive parameters, no mode switching — ablates mode-level contribution).

KEY ABLATIONS (6): (1) Mode switching value: FrontierLoop vs. B-STaR-enhanced STaR (same diagnostics for parameter tuning, no generation↔RL switching); (2) Adaptive vs. fixed cycling: FrontierLoop vs. SePT (same total compute, diagnostic vs. fixed scheduling); (3) Diagnostic signal comparison (SEG vs. entropy vs. DSFS vs. combined); (4) Targeted vs. uniform difficulty in generation; (5) With vs. without collapse prevention; (6) Compute efficiency: H100-hours per percentage point.

EVALUATION: MATH-500, AIME 2024, LiveCodeBench. Report pass@1, pass@32, per-difficulty breakdowns, compute efficiency, number of adaptive cycles, mode switches, collapse events. Report Cover@tau for reasoning reliability.

The CRITICAL COMPARISON is FrontierLoop vs. SePT (fixed cycling) and FrontierLoop vs. B-STaR-enhanced STaR (adaptive but single-paradigm). If FrontierLoop outperforms both: (a) adaptive scheduling beats fixed scheduling (vs. SePT) and (b) mode-level adaptation beats within-paradigm adaptation alone (vs. B-STaR).

COMPUTE ADVANTAGE: Self-improvement regime, no teacher. Diagnostic module adds ~15% overhead. Savings from: not generating redundant data when RL can consolidate (20-30% over SePT), early stopping on saturation/collapse, targeted generation at frontier difficulty.",

  "title": "FrontierLoop: Diagnostic-Guided Mode Scheduling Between Data Generation and RL for Mathematical Self-Improvement",
  "core_problem": "Self-improvement methods for mathematical reasoning — where the model generates its own synthetic training data and improves without an external teacher — make scheduling decisions at the WRONG LEVEL OF ABSTRACTION. Existing adaptive methods tune hyperparameters WITHIN a single training paradigm (B-STaR adjusts temperature and reward thresholds within SFT iterations, ICLR 2025; AdaSTaR adjusts data sampling priorities within STaR, NeurIPS 2025), but the higher-level question of WHICH training paradigm to use at any given moment remains unanswered.

This matters because self-improvement involves two fundamentally different computational activities with different properties:

(1) DATA GENERATION (Support Expansion): Creating new synthetic training data — reasoning traces for existing problems (STaR-style) or entirely new problems (MathSmith/Absolute Zero-style). This is inference-only compute, expands the model's behavioral support (Unified View, arXiv 2604.07941), and its value depends on whether the current data pool has been exhausted.

(2) RL TRAINING (Policy Reshaping): Consolidating latent capabilities into reliable pass@1 performance via GRPO. This is gradient compute, reshapes the policy within the currently reachable behavior space, and its value depends on whether there is still a gap between what the model CAN do (pass@k) and what it reliably DOES (pass@1).

The optimal balance between these modes changes as the model improves, but no existing method adapts this balance:

- FIXED-PARADIGM METHODS (STaR, ReST-EM, SePT): Generate data, train, repeat on a fixed schedule. SePT (arXiv 2510.18814) alternates generation and SFT in fixed 3-epoch cycles without diagnostic guidance. ReST-EM observes diminishing returns after 2-3 iterations without understanding whether to generate more data or switch to RL.

- WITHIN-PARADIGM ADAPTIVE METHODS (B-STaR, AdaSTaR): Adapt hyperparameters within STaR/SFT. B-STaR (ICLR 2025) monitors exploration/exploitation via a balance score and adjusts temperature (0.5-1.2) and reward threshold — powerful levers WITHIN the SFT paradigm. But B-STaR cannot switch to RL training when the Sampling Efficiency Gap indicates consolidation would be more productive, and cannot generate new problems when its fixed training set is exhausted. AdaSTaR (NeurIPS 2025) uses solve-rate signals for adaptive data sampling with 58.6% FLOPs reduction — but adjusts WHICH data to sample, not WHETHER to generate new data or train differently.

- WITHIN-RL ADAPTIVE METHODS (SwS, SEC, SIRI): Adapt within RL training. SwS (NeurIPS 2025, arXiv 2506.08989) identifies weaknesses during RL and synthesizes targeted problems — but performs synthesis continuously, not diagnostically triggered. SIRI cycles rollout length within RL. SEC uses MAB for category selection within RL.

- CONTINUOUS SYNTHESIS (SvS): Synthesizes new problems at every RLVR step regardless of need, wasting compute when the current data pool is sufficient.

The key insight is that RL and data generation have COMPLEMENTARY failure modes: RL saturates when pass@k plateaus (it cannot expand the frontier beyond the base model's latent capabilities, arXiv 2504.13837), while data generation is wasteful when the model hasn't consolidated its existing knowledge (large Sampling Efficiency Gap means RL can still improve pass@1 without new data). The DIAGNOSTIC TOOLS to detect these states already exist — pass@64 predicts RL outcomes (Quagmires: R²=0.87 on Llama3-8B, arXiv 2510.01624), entropy trajectory signals collapse (Entrocraft, arXiv 2604.26326), and the generation-verification gap determines self-improvement ceilings (Mind the Gap, ICLR 2025) — but they have never been used for MODE-LEVEL scheduling between fundamentally different training regimes.",
  "opportunity": "We propose FrontierLoop: the first framework that uses diagnostic signals for MODE-LEVEL scheduling — switching between fundamentally different training regimes (data generation vs. RL) — in mathematical self-improvement. This extends prior work on within-paradigm adaptation (B-STaR's parameter adjustment, AdaSTaR's data selection) to the higher-level orchestration decision that determines the training regime itself.

The hierarchy of adaptive self-improvement decisions clarifies FrontierLoop's contribution:

Level 1 — TOKEN/GROUP-LEVEL: Pass@k Training (arXiv 2508.10751) computes group-level advantages to balance exploration/exploitation within single RL steps.
Level 2 — DATA-LEVEL: AdaSTaR adjusts which training examples to sample within iterations; HS-STaR targets boundary-difficulty problems; SAI-DPO (ACL 2026 Findings, arXiv 2505.16176) recalibrates instance selection using pass-rate difficulty.
Level 3 — PARAMETER-LEVEL: B-STaR adjusts temperature and reward thresholds across STaR iterations.
Level 4 — WITHIN-MODE: SwS synthesizes targeted problems within RL; SEC selects problem categories within RL; SIRI varies rollout length within RL.
Level 5 — MODE-LEVEL (FrontierLoop): Switches between fundamentally different computational regimes — inference-only data generation vs. gradient-based RL training — with different compute profiles, optimization objectives, and data requirements.

Four specific gaps at Level 5 create FrontierLoop's opportunity:

(a) NO MODE SWITCHING: B-STaR (ICLR 2025) is the strongest existing diagnostic-adaptive method, but it operates entirely within online RFT (SFT). It adjusts sampling temperature and reward threshold to balance exploration/exploitation — powerful levers within SFT. But B-STaR cannot switch to RL training when the Sampling Efficiency Gap indicates consolidation would be more productive, and cannot generate new problems when its fixed training set is exhausted. FrontierLoop adds the mode-switching capability that B-STaR lacks.

(b) FIXED-SCHEDULE CYCLING: SePT (arXiv 2510.18814) demonstrates that alternating between self-generation and training improves reasoning (Pass@1: 22.7→39.5 on Qwen2.5-Math-7B), but uses fixed 3-epoch cycles without diagnostics. Generation phases may occur when RL could still consolidate existing knowledge; training phases may continue past saturation. FrontierLoop replaces SePT's fixed schedule with diagnostic-triggered transitions.

(c) NO CROSS-MODE DIAGNOSTICS: SwS (NeurIPS 2025) diagnoses weaknesses WITHIN RL to guide problem synthesis, and B-STaR diagnoses exploration/exploitation WITHIN SFT to adjust parameters. But no method uses diagnostics to decide WHICH mode is currently most productive. When B-STaR detects declining exploration, its only lever is temperature — it cannot decide that switching to RL would be more effective.

(d) NO GENERATION-VERIFICATION GAP STOPPING: SOAR (arXiv 2601.18778) uses bilevel meta-RL where a teacher copy generates problems based on measured student progress, but requires a separate teacher-student architecture. The solver-verifier gap theory (arXiv 2507.00075) models self-improvement as an exponential curve toward a computable limit, but no method uses this for principled stopping of the overall self-improvement loop.

FrontierLoop's value proposition is COMPUTE EFFICIENCY through mode-appropriate scheduling: generate data only when diagnostics indicate frontier exhaustion (saving 20-30% over SePT's fixed generation), target generation at specific difficulty bands where the model is stuck, and consolidate via RL only when the Sampling Efficiency Gap indicates room for pass@1 improvement.",
  "landscape": "FOUNDATIONAL SELF-IMPROVEMENT METHODS:

STaR (arXiv 2203.14465, NeurIPS 2022, Zelikman et al.) generates chain-of-thought rationales, filters for correctness, and fine-tunes iteratively. Includes 'rationalization' for failed problems. FrontierLoop extends STaR's generate→filter→train loop with diagnostic-guided mode scheduling and RL-based consolidation.

ReST-EM (Beyond Human Data, arXiv 2312.06585, Google DeepMind, 2023) formalizes self-training as Expectation-Maximization. Critical observation: diminishing returns after 2-3 iterations. FrontierLoop uses diagnostics to distinguish genuine saturation from suboptimal data targeting.

V-STaR (arXiv 2402.06457, 2024) trains a DPO-based verifier on both correct and incorrect STaR solutions. FrontierLoop could incorporate V-STaR's verifier for enhanced filtering during generation phases.

DIAGNOSTIC-ADAPTIVE SELF-IMPROVEMENT — CLOSEST PRIOR WORK:

B-STaR (arXiv 2412.17256, ICLR 2025, HKUST) is the most directly relevant prior work. B-STaR monitors exploration (Pass@K, Pass@K-S, distinct equations) and exploitation (Best-of-K accuracy, Reward@K-S) across STaR iterations, computing a balance score bs_i = min(n'_i/n*, 1)·(n'_i/n_i) to autonomously adjust sampling temperature (0.5-1.2) and reward threshold (-1.0 to 1.0). It does not generate new problems, does not incorporate RL training, and cannot switch between training modes. Its adaptation is at Level 3 (parameter adjustment); FrontierLoop operates at Level 5 (mode switching). B-STaR's insights are complementary — FrontierLoop could use B-STaR-style parameter adaptation WITHIN each mode while adding higher-level mode scheduling.

AdaSTaR (arXiv 2505.16322, NeurIPS 2025, Koh et al.) addresses data imbalance in STaR through adaptive sampling: a hierarchical min-heap priority system orders observations by last-sampled iteration and win-rate, with a curriculum component using training accuracy α as strength proxy (quadratic f(α)=α² for automatic difficulty scheduling). FrontierLoop's difficulty-stratified generation targeting extends AdaSTaR's adaptive sampling from within-iteration data selection to cross-mode generation decisions.

SAI-DPO (arXiv 2505.16176, ACL 2026 Findings) uses pass-rate-derived difficulty metrics and knowledge semantic alignment for iterative DPO training recalibration, achieving ~6 point improvements on AIME24. Operates within DPO training; FrontierLoop extends pass-rate-based adaptation to mode-level scheduling.

GENERATION↔TRAINING CYCLING METHODS:

SePT (arXiv 2510.18814, 'A Model Can Help Itself,' 2025) is the key ablation baseline. SePT alternates between self-generation (low-temperature sampling) and SFT training in FIXED 3-epoch cycles with online data refresh — each new batch from the most recently updated model. Temperature annealed 0.6→1.0. On Qwen2.5-Math-7B: Pass@1/8/32 of 39.5/57.7/67.9 (from 22.7/47.3/61.0 baseline). CRITICAL: SePT proves generation↔training cycling works but uses NO diagnostic guidance. It is the direct 'non-adaptive' version of FrontierLoop — showing FrontierLoop outperforms SePT demonstrates the value of diagnostic-guided mode scheduling.

SIRI (arXiv 2509.25176, 2025) performs 3 iterations of compression↔expansion cycling WITHIN RL, oscillating rollout length 8,192↔16,384 tokens via cosine scheduler. AIME24: 40.4% (vs. 28.2%) with 46.9% token reduction. SIRI cycles WITHIN RL (varying rollout length); FrontierLoop cycles BETWEEN modes (generation vs. RL).

ReMiT (arXiv 2602.03075, Feb 2026) performs iterative mid-training↔RL cycling across two cycles, validating that iterative cycling compounds.

WITHIN-RL PROBLEM SYNTHESIS:

SwS (arXiv 2506.08989, NeurIPS 2025) identifies questions the model consistently fails during RL, extracts core concepts, and synthesizes targeted problems. 10.0% avg improvement on 7B, 7.7% on 32B across 8 benchmarks. DIFFERENTIATION: SwS synthesizes WITHIN RL based on binary failure detection; FrontierLoop uses diagnostics for mode-level decisions (WHEN to synthesize at all) using multiple signals (pass@k spectrum, difficulty stratification, entropy).

Beyond Pass@1 / SvS (arXiv 2508.14029, 2025) synthesizes variational problems during RLVR, +18.3%/+22.8% pass@32 on AIME24/25. Continuous synthesis at every step; FrontierLoop's diagnostic-gated generation saves compute when current data is sufficient.

SOAR (arXiv 2601.18778, Meta FAIR/MIT/NYU, Jan 2026) uses bilevel meta-RL: a teacher COPY generates problems for a student copy, rewarded by measured student progress on hard problems (0/128 success rate). DIFFERENTIATION: SOAR requires separate teacher-student architecture; FrontierLoop uses a single model with diagnostic signals, lower compute overhead.

SELF-PLAY AND ZERO-DATA METHODS:

Absolute Zero (arXiv 2505.03335, 2025) achieves SOTA with zero external data via self-play. R-Zero (arXiv 2508.05004, 2025) uses Challenger-Solver co-evolution. R-Diverse (arXiv 2602.13103, Feb 2026) addresses 'Diversity Illusion.' FrontierLoop is generation-mechanism agnostic — self-play, sampling, or synthesis — with diagnostics determining which is productive.

DIAGNOSTIC TOOLS AND SIGNALS:

Quagmires (arXiv 2510.01624, NeurIPS 2025 MATH-AI Workshop) trained hundreds of models up to 12B: pass@64 predicts RL outcomes with R²=0.87, generalization loss achieves R²=0.88, combined predictor R²=0.94 (all on Llama3-8B-Instruct). Used as STATIC pre-RL predictor; FrontierLoop extends to DYNAMIC mode scheduling.

Pass@k Training (arXiv 2508.10751, ByteDance/RUC) uses pass@k as a GROUP-LEVEL reward signal: groups k responses, assigns positive reward if at least one correct, distributes group advantage to all k responses. 17.9% vs. 12.9% Pass@1 on Enigmata (Qwen2.5-7B). Validates pass@k as active signal at group-level granularity; FrontierLoop uses pass@k at phase-level diagnostic granularity for mode switching.

Entrocraft (arXiv 2604.26326, 2026) achieves ~17% improvement in pass@32 via entropy-guided rejection sampling. EntroPIC (arXiv 2511.15248, 2025) uses PID control for entropy stabilization. Both validate entropy trajectory as training stability diagnostic.

Cover@tau (arXiv 2510.08325, 2025) measures reasoning reliability beyond pass@k.

SELF-IMPROVEMENT THEORY:

Mind the Gap (arXiv 2412.02674, ICLR 2025) formalizes self-improvement through the generation-verification gap, scaling monotonically with pre-training compute. Provides FrontierLoop's stopping criterion.

Solver-Verifier Gap Theory (arXiv 2507.00075, 2025) models self-improvement as exponential curve toward computable limit. Key: external data can be introduced at any stage — supporting FrontierLoop's flexible scheduling.

'Can Large Reasoning Models Self-Train?' (arXiv 2505.21444) shows self-training improves then collapses via reward hacking. FrontierLoop's collapse detection addresses this.

Does RL Really Incentivize Reasoning Beyond the Base Model? (arXiv 2504.13837, NeurIPS 2025 Best Paper Runner-Up) shows RLVR improves pass@1 but does NOT expand pass@k frontier — FrontierLoop's central motivation for diagnostic-triggered generation.

DART-Math (arXiv 2407.13690, NeurIPS 2024) identifies easy-query bias. HS-STaR (arXiv 2505.19866, EMNLP 2025) targets boundary problems. SEC (arXiv 2505.14970, 2025) uses MAB for curriculum within RL. MathSmith (arXiv 2508.05592, 2025) optimizes problem generation via RL. HSIR (arXiv 2605.24998, May 2026) improves within-iteration efficiency. All composable with FrontierLoop.

# Pass@k Analysis: Key Findings

## Vanishing Learning Signal

The paper demonstrates that **pass@k provides diminishing gradient signals precisely when exploration is most needed**. The authors show this objective "provides a vanishing learning signal in regimes where exploration is most critical."

## Exploration Collapse Dynamics

The research identifies a critical phenomenon where the performance gap between pass@k and pass@1 shrinks as the policy concentrates its probability mass. This means that as training progresses and the model becomes more confident, the advantage of sampling multiple solutions diminishes.

## Diagnostic vs. Optimization Tool

The core argument distinguishes between two roles:

- **As diagnostic**: Pass@k remains "a useful diagnostic tool" for measuring model capabilities
- **As optimization objective**: It "may be an unsuitable direct objective for optimization"

## Root Mechanism

The authors' mathematical analysis reveals that pass@k fundamentally functions as "per-example positive reweighting of the simpler pass@1 objective." This reframing explains why it fails to adequately incentivize exploration during reinforcement learning.

## Recommendation

Rather than optimizing pass@k directly, the paper advocates for "mechanisms explicitly encouraging efficient exploration" as a more effective approach for reasoning tasks in RLVR (Reinforcement Learning with Verification and Reasoning).

# RL Squeezes, SFT Expands: Paper Analysis

**Title:** "RL Squeezes, SFT Expands: A Comparative Study of Reasoning LLMs"

**Authors:** Kohsei Matsutani, Shota Takashiro, Gouki Minegishi, Takeshi Kojima, Yusuke Iwasawa, and Yutaka Matsuo

## Key Findings on Complementary Effects

The research demonstrates that reinforcement learning and supervised fine-tuning produce opposing effects on reasoning patterns:

**RL's Concentrating Effect:**
The paper shows that "RL compresses incorrect trajectories" while steepening decay rates approximately 2.5 times across step-level metrics. This means reinforcement learning focuses reasoning functionality into a small subset of high-value reasoning steps.

**SFT's Diversifying Effect:**
Conversely, "SFT expands correct ones" (trajectories) and flattens decay rates to roughly one-third of their original values. This indicates supervised fine-tuning distributes reasoning capacity across many steps more evenly.

## Supporting Evidence

The researchers employed two-level analysis:
- **Trajectory-level:** Clustering unique reasoning paths showed how each method reshapes the complete reasoning process
- **Step-level:** Graph analysis measured node visitation frequency, degree, and betweenness centrality distributions

These complementary mechanisms explain why the current training paradigm—SFT followed by RL—succeeds: SFT broadens the reasoning foundation while RL refines and concentrates it toward optimal solutions.

## Entrocraft: Entropy Curve Control for LLM RL

Entrocraft is a rejection-sampling approach that realizes user-customized entropy schedules by biasing the advantage distributions. It requires no objective regularization and is advantage-estimator-agnostic.

### Key Performance Improvements

Entrocraft enables a 4B model to outperform an 8B baseline, sustains improvement for up to 4x longer before plateauing, and raises pass@K by 50% over the baseline. These improvements address a critical issue in LLM reinforcement learning: most RL algorithms suffer from performance saturation, preventing further gains as RL training scales, which can be characterized by the collapse of entropy, a key diagnostic for exploration in RL.

### Technical Approach

Entrocraft enables a systematic study of entropy schedules, where linear annealing, which starts high and decays to a slightly lower target, performs best. Theoretically, the method relates per-step entropy change to the advantage distribution under minimal assumptions, which explains the behavior of existing RL and entropy-preserving methods.

### Broader Impacts

Entrocraft addresses performance saturation, significantly improving generalization, output diversity, and long-term training.

# ReLIFT: Key Technical Details

## 1) Switching Mechanism & Buffer Threshold

**Trigger**: The system switches from RL to SFT when the fine-tuning buffer accumulates enough examples. Specifically: "When the size of the fine-tuning buffer exceeds a predefined threshold M (i.e., |BufferFT|≥M), we sample a batch of M (q,s) pairs."

**Buffer Threshold M**: The default is set to batch size. The ablation study (Appendix H) tests M values of 32, 64, 128, and 256, with M=64 showing optimal performance.

## 2) Solution Source

**External Teacher Models**: The approach uses DeepSeek-R1 as the demonstration source for reproducibility. However, the authors note this "does not imply that ReLIFT is a distillation method." They state: "the framework is equally applicable to other data sources, such as human expert annotators."

Solutions are obtained "either by collecting them in advance before training or by consulting a stronger model."

## 3) Exact Benchmark Results

**Qwen2.5-Math-7B Performance** (Table 1):
- AIME-24: 28.3%
- AIME-25: 22.9%
- AMC: 65.1%
- MATH-500: 87.9%
- OlympiadBench: 57.3%
- MMLU-Pro: 53.9%
- **Overall: 52.6%**

## 4) Interleaving Type

**Adaptive Interleaving**: The authors describe it as having "adaptive frequency"—"Early in training, when the model's performance is low, SFT is applied more frequently to accelerate learning. As training progresses and the model improves, RL is prioritized."

This contrasts with ablation variants: ReLIFT(uniform) applies FT at fixed intervals; ReLIFT(random) uses random scheduling—both perform worse.

## 5) Hard Problem Identification

**Mechanism**: Questions are classified as "hardest" when "acc(q)=0"—meaning the model generates zero correct answers across rollout samples. The paper uses this binary threshold rather than a probabilistic measure.

Difficulty stratification: Easy (≥75% accuracy), Medium (37.5-62.5%), Hard (12.5-25%), Hardest (0%).

## 6) Demonstration Requirements

**"13% of Demonstration Data" Clarification**: ReLIFT uses 8,640 demonstration samples versus SFT's 46,000 (from OpenR1-Math-46k dataset). This represents approximately 18.8%—though the paper states ReLIFT achieves results "with significantly less demonstration data."

**GPU Hours Comparison** (Table 2):
- SFT: 8×8 GPU hours
- ReLIFT: 52×8 GPU hours
- LUFFY: 73×8 GPU hours

ReLIFT requires fewer demonstrations than full-scale baselines while maintaining computational efficiency.

## Overview

Large language models (LLMs) are typically trained by reinforcement learning (RL) with verifiable rewards (RLVR) and supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on reasoning traces to improve their reasoning abilities. The paper introduces a novel analysis framework that quantifies reasoning paths and captures their qualitative changes under each training process (with models of 1.5B, 7B, and 14B parameters on mathematical domains).

## Methodology

The paper investigates the reasoning process at two levels of granularity: the trajectory-level, which examines complete reasoning outputs, and the step-level, which analyzes reasoning graphs whose nodes correspond to individual reasoning steps.

## Key Findings

Clustering of unique reasoning trajectories shows complementary effects: RL compresses incorrect trajectories, whereas SFT expands correct ones. This suggests that the two training approaches have distinct and complementary roles in shaping how reasoning models generate solutions.

The paper was authored by Kohsei Matsutani, Shota Takashiro, Gouki Minegishi, Takeshi Kojima, Yusuke Iwasawa, and Yutaka Matsuo, and was published on September 25, 2025.

# ProRL's Frontier Expansion Claims: Detailed Analysis

## 1) 100% Pass Rate on Zero-Score Tasks

**YES - Explicitly Claimed:**
The paper states: "many tasks where the base model fails to produce any correct solutions regardless of the amount of sampling, while our RL-trained model achieves 100% pass rates" (Figure 4 caption). However, specific task identifiers aren't universally named—the paper references this pattern across logical puzzles and out-of-distribution challenges without exhaustively listing every instance.

## 2) Specific Tasks/Benchmarks Showing Frontier Expansion

**Confirmed examples:**
- **Boxnet (OOD)**: Base model scored 0.00%; ProRL achieved 7.91%
- **Game of Life Halting (OOD)**: Base 3.49% → ProRL 52.29%
- **Family Relationships (Logic)**: Distribution shifted from predominantly zero accuracy to peaking at perfect accuracy
- **Graph Coloring**: Sustained improvements across increased difficulty levels (10+ nodes)
- **Reasoning Gym Logical Puzzles**: Average improvement of 54.8%

## 3) Claimed Conditions for Expansion

Three essential components:

1. **Prolonged Training**: "more than 2k training steps" (exceeding prior work's "hundreds of steps")
2. **KL Divergence Control**: Explicit regularization preventing policy drift while maintaining entropy
3. **Reference Policy Resetting**: Periodic hard-resets of reference model and optimizer states to avoid premature convergence

Additional factor: Task diversity across five domains (math, code, STEM, logic puzzles, instruction-following).

## 4) Reconciliation with arXiv:2504.13837

The paper doesn't cite or address that specific work. Instead, it engages with Dang et al. (2025) and Yang Yue et al. (2025) arguments against RL frontier expansion. ProRL's counter-argument: prior studies suffered from "(1) overreliance on specialized domains like mathematics...restricting exploration; (2) premature termination of RL training before models can fully explore." The proposed resolution is **sustained, multi-domain training**.

## 5) Expansion: Task-Specific or General?

**PREDOMINANTLY TASK-SPECIFIC:**

The paper identifies three patterns:
- **Diminish**: Tasks where base models excel show narrowed reasoning diversity
- **Plateau**: Early saturation of RL gains
- **Sustained**: Complex tasks requiring extensive exploration benefit most

Finding: "The weaker the start, the stronger the gain with ProRL"—frontier expansion correlates inversely with base model performance on that task.

## 6) Model Sizes Tested

**Primary focus: 1.5B parameter model only**

- Nemotron-Research-Reasoning-Qwen-1.5B (main contribution)
- Compared against DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B (base) and DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B (reference)
- No systematic scaling study across multiple model sizes reported

This matters because self-improvement involves two fundamentally different computational activities with different properties:

(1) DATA GENERATION (Support Expansion): Creating new synthetic training data — reasoning traces for existing problems (STaR-style) or entirely new problems (MathSmith/Absolute Zero-style).   "core_problem": "Self-improvement methods for mathematical reasoning — where the model generates its own synthetic training data and improves without an external teacher — make scheduling decisions at the WRONG LEVEL OF ABSTRACTION. Existing adaptive methods tune hyperparameters WITHIN a single training paradigm (B-STaR adjusts temperature and reward thresholds within SFT iterations, ICLR 2025; AdaSTaR adjusts data sampling priorities within STaR, NeurIPS 2025), but the higher-level question of WHICH training paradigm to use at any given moment remains unanswered.

This matters because self-improvement involves two fundamentally different computational activities with different properties:

(1) DATA GENERATION (Support Expansion): Creating new synthetic training data — reasoning traces for existing problems (STaR-style) or entirely new problems (MathSmith/Absolute Zero-style). This is inference-only compute, expands the model's behavioral support (Unified View, arXiv 2604.07941), and its value depends on whether the current data pool has been exhausted.

(2) RL TRAINING (Policy Reshaping): Consolidating latent capabilities into reliable pass@1 performance via GRPO. This is gradient compute, reshapes the policy within the currently reachable behavior space, and its value depends on whether there is still a gap between what the model CAN do (pass@k) and what it reliably DOES (pass@1).

Empirical evidence now strongly supports these as complementary modes: 'RL Squeezes, SFT Expands' (arXiv 2509.21128) demonstrates through trajectory-level clustering and step-level graph analysis that RL compresses incorrect trajectories (steepening decay rates ~2.5x) while SFT expands correct ones (flattening decay rates to ~1/3). This directly validates the design motivation for alternating between these fundamentally different training regimes.

The optimal balance between these modes changes as the model improves, but no existing method in the SELF-IMPROVEMENT regime adaptively schedules this balance:

- FIXED-PARADIGM METHODS (STaR, ReST-EM, SePT): Generate data, train, repeat on a fixed schedule. SePT (arXiv 2510.18814) alternates generation and SFT in fixed 3-epoch cycles without diagnostic guidance. ReST-EM observes diminishing returns after 2-3 iterations without understanding whether to generate more data or switch to RL.

- FIXED-SCHEDULE CYCLING WITH RL (RLoop): RLoop (arXiv 2511.04285) cycles RL to RFT on a fixed schedule (200 RL steps then 1 epoch RFT, 3 iterations) to address 'RL overfitting' — policy over-specialization and catastrophic forgetting of diverse solutions. On Qwen-2.5-7b-Math, achieves AIME 2024 pass@32 of 73.33% and MATH pass@32 of 80.00%, a 15%+ improvement over vanilla RL. RLoop demonstrates that RL-RFT cycling is effective, but its FIXED schedule cannot adapt to model state — it applies the same 200-step/1-epoch rhythm regardless of whether RL has saturated or still has room to consolidate.

- WITHIN-PARADIGM ADAPTIVE METHODS (B-STaR, AdaSTaR): Adapt hyperparameters within STaR/SFT. B-STaR (ICLR 2025) monitors exploration/exploitation via a balance score and adjusts temperature (0.5-1.2) and reward threshold — powerful levers WITHIN the SFT paradigm. But B-STaR cannot switch to RL training when the Sampling Efficiency Gap indicates consolidation would be more productive, and cannot generate new problems when its fixed training set is exhausted. SIRI cycles rollout length within RL. SEC uses MAB for category selection within RL.

This achieves +6.7 points average across 6 benchmarks. However, ReLIFT uses EXTERNAL teacher solutions (DeepSeek-R1) for SFT phases — it is not self-improvement. Its switching operates at the SAMPLE level (per-problem difficulty routing) rather than the PHASE level (diagnostic-triggered mode transitions). FrontierLoop differs on three axes: (1) self-improvement regime (no external teacher), (2) phase-level mode switching (not per-sample routing), (3) multi-signal diagnostics (not binary acc=0 threshold).

- CONTINUOUS SYNTHESIS (SvS): Synthesizes new problems at every RLVR step regardless of need, wasting compute when the current data pool is sufficient.

The key insight is that RL and data generation have COMPLEMENTARY failure modes: RL saturates when pass@k plateaus (under standard RLVR conditions, RL does not expand the pass@k frontier — arXiv 2504.13837, NeurIPS 2025 Best Paper Runner-Up), while data generation is wasteful when the model hasn't consolidated its existing knowledge (large Sampling Efficiency Gap means RL can still improve pass@1 without new data). FrontierLoop is most valuable in the STANDARD RLVR regime where the frontier-expansion limitation is empirically well-documented, while remaining compatible with prolonged-training setups where generation phases serve to diversify rather than expand frontiers.

The DIAGNOSTIC TOOLS to detect these states already exist — pass@64 predicts RL outcomes (Quagmires: R-squared=0.87 on Llama3-8B, arXiv 2510.01624), entropy trajectory signals collapse (Entrocraft, arXiv 2604.26326), and the generation-verification gap determines self-improvement ceilings (Mind the Gap, ICLR 2025) — but they have never been used for MODE-LEVEL scheduling between fundamentally different training regimes.",
  "opportunity": "We propose FrontierLoop: the first framework that uses diagnostic signals for MODE-LEVEL scheduling — switching between fundamentally different training regimes (data generation vs. RL) — in mathematical self-improvement. This extends prior work on within-paradigm adaptation (B-STaR's parameter adjustment, AdaSTaR's data selection) to the higher-level orchestration decision that determines the training regime itself.

The hierarchy of adaptive self-improvement decisions clarifies FrontierLoop's contribution:

Level 1 — TOKEN/GROUP-LEVEL: Pass@k Training (arXiv 2508.10751) computes group-level advantages to balance exploration/exploitation within single RL steps.
Level 2 — DATA-LEVEL: AdaSTaR adjusts which training examples to sample within iterations; HS-STaR targets boundary-difficulty problems; SAI-DPO (ACL 2026 Findings, arXiv 2505.16176) recalibrates instance selection using pass-rate difficulty.
Level 3 — PARAMETER-LEVEL: B-STaR adjusts temperature and reward thresholds across STaR iterations.
Level 4 — WITHIN-MODE: SwS synthesizes targeted problems within RL; SEC selects problem categories within RL; SIRI varies rollout length within RL.
Level 5 — MODE-LEVEL (FrontierLoop): Switches between fundamentally different computational regimes — inference-only data generation vs. gradient-based RL training — with different compute profiles, optimization objectives, and data requirements.

Five specific gaps at Level 5 create FrontierLoop's opportunity:

(a) NO ADAPTIVE MODE SWITCHING IN SELF-IMPROVEMENT: B-STaR (ICLR 2025) is the strongest existing diagnostic-adaptive method, but it operates entirely within online RFT (SFT). But B-STaR cannot switch to RL training when the Sampling Efficiency Gap indicates consolidation would be more productive, and cannot generate new problems when its fixed training set is exhausted. FrontierLoop adds the mode-switching capability that B-STaR lacks.

(b) FIXED-SCHEDULE CYCLING WITHOUT DIAGNOSTICS: Both SePT (arXiv 2510.18814, generation-SFT cycling with fixed 3-epoch cycles, Pass@1: 22.7 to 39.5 on Qwen2.5-Math-7B) and RLoop (arXiv 2511.04285, RL-RFT cycling with fixed 200-step/1-epoch schedule, AIME 2024 pass@32: 73.33% on Qwen-2.5-7b-Math) demonstrate that cycling between training modes improves reasoning. But both use FIXED schedules without diagnostics. Generation/RFT phases may occur when RL could still consolidate existing knowledge; RL phases may continue past saturation. FrontierLoop replaces fixed schedules with diagnostic-triggered transitions.

(c) ADAPTIVE INTERLEAVING REQUIRES EXTERNAL TEACHER: ReLIFT (arXiv 2506.07527, ICLR 2026) achieves adaptive RL-SFT interleaving with a buffer-based switching mechanism and shows it outperforms fixed scheduling. But ReLIFT requires an external teacher (DeepSeek-R1) for SFT solutions and operates at the per-sample level (routing individual hard problems to SFT). FrontierLoop brings adaptive mode switching to the SELF-IMPROVEMENT regime — no external teacher, phase-level diagnostics, and multi-signal scheduling rather than binary difficulty thresholds.

The solver-verifier gap theory (arXiv 2507.00075) models self-improvement as an exponential curve toward a computable limit, but no method uses this for principled stopping of the overall self-improvement loop.

STaR (arXiv 2203.14465, NeurIPS 2022, Zelikman et al.) generates chain-of-thought rationales, filters for correctness, and fine-tunes iteratively. Includes 'rationalization' for failed problems. FrontierLoop extends STaR's generate-filter-train loop with diagnostic-guided mode scheduling and RL-based consolidation.

ReST-EM (Beyond Human Data, arXiv 2312.06585, Google DeepMind, 2023) formalizes self-training as Expectation-Maximization. Critical observation: diminishing returns after 2-3 iterations. FrontierLoop uses diagnostics to distinguish genuine saturation from suboptimal data targeting.

V-STaR (arXiv 2402.06457, 2024) trains a DPO-based verifier on both correct and incorrect STaR solutions. FrontierLoop could incorporate V-STaR's verifier for enhanced filtering during generation phases.

B-STaR (arXiv 2412.17256, ICLR 2025, HKUST) is the most directly relevant prior work within single-paradigm adaptation. B-STaR monitors exploration (Pass@K, Pass@K-S, distinct equations) and exploitation (Best-of-K accuracy, Reward@K-S) across STaR iterations, computing a balance score bs_i = min(n'_i/n*, 1) times (n'_i/n_i) to autonomously adjust sampling temperature (0.5-1.2) and reward threshold (-1.0 to 1.0). On Mistral-7B, achieves GSM8K 53.8 and MATH 27.8 over 9 iterations. CRITICAL DIFFERENTIATION: B-STaR adapts parameters WITHIN a single training paradigm (online RFT/SFT). It does not generate new problems, does not incorporate RL training, and cannot switch between training modes. Its adaptation is at Level 3 (parameter adjustment); FrontierLoop operates at Level 5 (mode switching). B-STaR's insights are complementary — FrontierLoop could use B-STaR-style parameter adaptation WITHIN each mode while adding higher-level mode scheduling.

AdaSTaR (arXiv 2505.16322, NeurIPS 2025, Koh et al.) addresses data imbalance in STaR through adaptive sampling: a hierarchical min-heap priority system orders observations by last-sampled iteration and win-rate, with a curriculum component using training accuracy alpha as strength proxy (quadratic f(alpha)=alpha-squared for automatic difficulty scheduling). Achieves best accuracy on 6/6 benchmarks with 58.6% average FLOPs reduction. DIFFERENTIATION: AdaSTaR adapts WHICH data to sample (Level 2), not WHETHER to generate new data or switch training paradigms (Level 5). FrontierLoop's difficulty-stratified generation targeting extends AdaSTaR's adaptive sampling from within-iteration data selection to cross-mode generation decisions.

SAI-DPO (arXiv 2505.16176, ACL 2026 Findings) uses pass-rate-derived difficulty metrics and knowledge semantic alignment for iterative DPO training recalibration, achieving ~6 point improvements on AIME24. Operates within DPO training; FrontierLoop extends pass-rate-based adaptation to mode-level scheduling.

GENERATION-TRAINING CYCLING METHODS — KEY BASELINES:

SePT (arXiv 2510.18814, 'A Model Can Help Itself,' 2025) is a key ablation baseline. SePT alternates between self-generation (low-temperature sampling) and SFT training in FIXED 3-epoch cycles with online data refresh — each new batch from the most recently updated model. Temperature annealed 0.6 to 1.0. On Qwen2.5-Math-7B: Pass@1/8/32 of 39.5/57.7/67.9 (from 22.7/47.3/61.0 baseline). CRITICAL: SePT proves generation-SFT cycling works but uses NO diagnostic guidance.

RLoop (arXiv 2511.04285, Zeng et al., Nov 2025) is the other key cycling baseline. RLoop addresses 'RL overfitting' — policy over-specialization and catastrophic forgetting of diverse solutions — via iterative RL-to-RFT cycling: 200 RL steps (DAPO algorithm) then filter successful trajectories into expert dataset then 1 epoch RFT to create superior policy initialization then repeat for 3 iterations. On Qwen-2.5-7b-Math: AIME 2024 pass@32 = 73.33%, MATH pass@32 = 80.00%, representing 9% average accuracy and 15%+ pass@32 improvement over vanilla RL. CRITICAL DIFFERENTIATION: RLoop's cycling is FIXED (200 steps/1 epoch per cycle, no diagnostics). It cannot detect whether RL has saturated early (wasting remaining steps) or still has room to consolidate (switching to RFT prematurely). RLoop demonstrates that RL-RFT cycling in self-improvement works; FrontierLoop adds diagnostic-guided adaptive scheduling to determine WHEN each mode transition is most productive. Together, SePT (generation-SFT, fixed) and RLoop (RL-RFT, fixed) establish that cycling works across different training paradigms, while FrontierLoop shows adaptive timing outperforms fixed schedules.

SIRI (arXiv 2509.25176, 2025) performs 3 iterations of compression-expansion cycling WITHIN RL, oscillating rollout length 8,192 to 16,384 tokens via cosine scheduler. AIME24: 40.4% (vs. 28.2%) with 46.9% token reduction. SIRI cycles WITHIN RL (varying rollout length); FrontierLoop cycles BETWEEN modes (generation vs. RL).

ReMiT (arXiv 2602.03075, Feb 2026) performs iterative mid-training to RL cycling across two cycles, validating that iterative cycling compounds.

ADAPTIVE INTERLEAVING WITH EXTERNAL DATA:

ReLIFT (arXiv 2506.07527, Ma et al., ICLR 2026) is the conceptually closest existing work to adaptive mode-switching. ReLIFT interleaves RL with targeted SFT for 'hardest questions' (acc(q)=0 in rollouts), using a buffer-based mechanism: hard problems accumulate in a buffer, and SFT is triggered when buffer size is at least threshold M (optimal M=64). Adaptive frequency — SFT more frequent early when model is weak, RL dominates as model improves. Achieves +6.7 points average across 6 benchmarks using only 13% of demonstration data. CRITICAL DIFFERENTIATION on three axes: (1) DATA SOURCE: ReLIFT uses external teacher solutions (DeepSeek-R1) — it is distillation-augmented, NOT self-improvement. (2) SWITCHING GRANULARITY: ReLIFT routes individual hard problems to SFT (per-sample switching); FrontierLoop makes phase-level mode transitions based on aggregate diagnostic signals. (3) SWITCHING SIGNAL: ReLIFT uses a binary threshold (acc=0 buffer count at least M=64); FrontierLoop uses multi-signal diagnostics (SEG, DSFS, entropy, SCD). ReLIFT validates that adaptive RL-SFT interleaving outperforms fixed scheduling — FrontierLoop brings this principle to the self-improvement regime with richer diagnostics.

WITHIN-RL PROBLEM SYNTHESIS:

SwS (arXiv 2506.08989, NeurIPS 2025) identifies questions the model consistently fails during RL, extracts core concepts, and synthesizes targeted problems. 10.0% avg improvement on 7B, 7.7% on 32B across 8 benchmarks. DIFFERENTIATION: SwS synthesizes WITHIN RL based on binary failure detection; FrontierLoop uses diagnostics for mode-level decisions (WHEN to synthesize at all) using multiple signals (pass@k spectrum, difficulty stratification, entropy).

Beyond Pass@1 / SvS (arXiv 2508.14029, 2025) synthesizes variational problems during RLVR, +18.3%/+22.8% pass@32 on AIME24/25. Continuous synthesis at every step; FrontierLoop's diagnostic-gated generation saves compute when current data is sufficient.

SOAR (arXiv 2601.18778, Meta FAIR/MIT/NYU, Jan 2026) uses bilevel meta-RL: a teacher COPY generates problems for a student copy, rewarded by measured student progress on hard problems (0/128 success rate). DIFFERENTIATION: SOAR requires separate teacher-student architecture; FrontierLoop uses a single model with diagnostic signals, lower compute overhead.

SELF-PLAY AND ZERO-DATA METHODS:

Absolute Zero (arXiv 2505.03335, 2025) achieves SOTA with zero external data via self-play. R-Zero (arXiv 2508.05004, 2025) uses Challenger-Solver co-evolution. R-Diverse (arXiv 2602.13103, Feb 2026) addresses 'Diversity Illusion.' FrontierLoop is generation-mechanism agnostic — self-play, sampling, or synthesis — with diagnostics determining which is productive.

EMPIRICAL EVIDENCE FOR COMPLEMENTARY MODES:

RL Squeezes, SFT Expands (arXiv 2509.21128, Matsutani et al., 2025) provides direct empirical support for FrontierLoop's core design motivation. This quantifies the complementary mechanisms: RL concentrates the policy around known-good solutions (consolidation), while SFT/generation broadens the reasoning foundation (expansion). FrontierLoop's mode scheduling directly operationalizes this complementarity — using diagnostics to determine when concentration (RL) vs. expansion (generation) is more productive.

RL FRONTIER EXPANSION — NUANCED PICTURE:

Does RL Really Incentivize Reasoning Beyond the Base Model? (arXiv 2504.13837, NeurIPS 2025 Best Paper Runner-Up) shows standard RLVR improves pass@1 but does NOT expand pass@k frontier — FrontierLoop's central motivation for diagnostic-triggered generation.

ProRL: Prolonged RL Expands Reasoning Boundaries (NeurIPS 2025, arXiv 2505.24864) demonstrates that under specific conditions — prolonged training (>2k steps), KL divergence control, reference policy resetting, and diverse multi-domain tasks — RL CAN discover novel strategies with 100% pass rates on tasks where base models score 0% (e.g., Boxnet: 0% to 7.91%, Game of Life Halting: 3.49% to 52.29%). Critically, frontier expansion correlates inversely with base model competence ('the weaker the start, the stronger the gain') and was only tested at 1.5B scale. RECONCILIATION: The frontier-expansion limitation is CONDITIONS-DEPENDENT. Under standard RLVR (short training, single math domain), arXiv 2504.13837's findings hold robustly. Under prolonged multi-domain training with KL control (ProRL), expansion occurs on specific tasks. FrontierLoop targets the standard RLVR regime where frontier limitations are well-documented; in prolonged-training setups, generation phases still serve valuable diversification (per 'RL Squeezes, SFT Expands').

DIAGNOSTIC TOOLS AND SIGNALS:

Quagmires (arXiv 2510.01624, NeurIPS 2025 MATH-AI Workshop) trained hundreds of models up to 12B: pass@64 predicts RL outcomes with R-squared=0.87, generalization loss achieves R-squared=0.88, combined predictor R-squared=0.94 (all on Llama3-8B-Instruct). Used as STATIC pre-RL predictor; FrontierLoop extends to DYNAMIC mode scheduling.

Pass@k Training (arXiv 2508.10751, ByteDance/RUC) uses pass@k as a GROUP-LEVEL reward signal: groups k responses, assigns positive reward if at least one correct, distributes group advantage to all k responses. 17.9% vs. 12.9% Pass@1 on Enigmata (Qwen2.5-7B). Validates pass@k as active signal at group-level granularity; FrontierLoop uses pass@k at phase-level diagnostic granularity for mode switching.

Pass@k as Diagnostic, Not Objective (arXiv 2511.16231, Nov 2025) demonstrates that pass@k provides a vanishing learning signal as the policy concentrates probability mass — it is fundamentally a per-example positive reweighting of pass@1. The paper validates pass@k as a useful DIAGNOSTIC tool while warning it is unsuitable as a direct OPTIMIZATION objective. This distinction directly supports FrontierLoop's design: we use SEG (pass@k minus pass@1) as a diagnostic signal for mode switching, not as an optimization objective. The known vanishing-signal phenomenon is additionally mitigated by FrontierLoop's compound criterion (SEG small AND pass@k stagnant), which distinguishes genuine frontier exhaustion from successful policy concentration.

Entrocraft (arXiv 2604.26326, 2026) raises pass@K by 50% relative over baseline via entropy-guided rejection sampling realizing user-customized entropy schedules (e.g., AIME-25 pass@32: 40.0% to 46.7% under GRPO to Entrocraft). EntroPIC (arXiv 2511.15248, 2025) uses PID control for entropy stabilization. Both validate entropy trajectory as training stability diagnostic.

Cover@tau (arXiv 2510.08325, 2025) measures reasoning reliability beyond pass@k.

SELF-IMPROVEMENT THEORY:

Mind the Gap (arXiv 2412.02674, ICLR 2025) formalizes self-improvement through the generation-verification gap, scaling monotonically with pre-training compute. Provides FrontierLoop's stopping criterion.

Solver-Verifier Gap Theory (arXiv 2507.00075, 2025) models self-improvement as exponential curve toward computable limit. Key: external data can be introduced at any stage — supporting FrontierLoop's flexible scheduling.

'Can Large Reasoning Models Self-Train?' (arXiv 2505.21444) shows self-training improves then collapses via reward hacking. FrontierLoop's collapse detection addresses this.

DART-Math (arXiv 2407.13690, NeurIPS 2024) identifies easy-query bias. HS-STaR (arXiv 2505.19866, EMNLP 2025) targets boundary problems. SEC (arXiv 2505.14970, 2025) uses MAB for curriculum within RL. MathSmith (arXiv 2508.05592, 2025) optimizes problem generation via RL.
